newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal's minority Socialist govt firmly in power.
newsitem.headline: Portugal's minority Socialist govt firmly in power.

text.p: Portugal's Socialists seem to have tightened their grip on power in the year since elections put them back in government, but without parliamentary control,
Opinion polls show the party has lost none of the backing it received in the October 1, 1995 general election when it ended a decade of rule by the conservative Social Democrats (PSD).

Analysts and commentators say Prime Minister Antonio Guterres can prepare for the delicate task of presenting a tough 1997 budget to win Portugal a place in the European Union's planned single currency, comfortable in the knowledge that he faces no real political threat.
"The government is still in its honeymoon...and everything points to 1997 also being a rosy year," wrote Diario Economico editor Nicolau Santos in an editorial on Tuesday.

In an interview with Reuters, the leader of the PSD, the main opposition group, said his party would back down if challenged by the government to unseat it over the budget plans, which are expected to be voted in November.
The Socialists have 112 seats in the 230-seat parliament to the PSD's 88 with the balance being divided equally between the Communists and the right-wing Popular Party.

PSD chief Marcelo Rebelo de Sousa said that his party's reluctance to bring about early elections was motivated by fears that political uncertainty could jeopardise Portugal's chances of qualifying for EMU.

But political commentators say that neither the PSD nor the other opposition parties are in shape for an electoral battle. The PSD is still recovering from the shock of being bundled out of government, while the Popular Party is riven by internal rivalries that forced the resignation of its leader last week.
"One year later, the opposition parties are just adrift," ran the headline in the Publico newspaper as it reviewed the past political year.

Rebelo de Sousa has even warned that he could follow Popular Party chief Manuel Monteiro and stand aside if the party's national congress this weekend rejects a series of internal reforms that he wants.
"You have to say that the lack of any real opposition has a lot to do with it (the Socialists' enduring popularity)," said one European diplomat.
There are regional elections later this month in the semi-autonomous Azores and Madeira islands but these have long been fiefdoms of the PSD and are not regarded as a serious political test.
The first real contest will be local authority polls in late 1997 -- when next year's budget measures are starting to bite.

On the credit side, the Socialists, who took power promising "rigour and a social conscience", have succeeded in pushing a 1996 deficit-cutting budget through parliament and seem well on the way to doing the same for the 1997 version.
The economy measures have been taken without stoking social tensions.

Guterres has also won praise for a more open style of government, including regular appearances in parliament to debate with the opposition -- something his austere PSD predecessor, Anibal Cavaco Silva, was reluctant to do.
But he has been accused of delaying more difficult political and economic decisions, including reform of the welfare system.
"The fact is that he (Guterres) has not really been put to a severe test yet. That could come next year," said the diplomat.
